extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of natural history, evolutionary biology, and anthropology (Victorian-era and modern historians/scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: Reading and critically assessing nineteenth-century evolutionary/anthropological arguments about causes of population change and the formation of human races, including use of empirical data, analogical reasoning, and alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative census comparison to infer population trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare successive census returns and compute rates of decrease (annual percentage), assuming uniform change between irregularly-spaced censuses where necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin presents native-population counts for several years (1832, 1836, 1853, 1860, 1866, 1872) and derives 'annual rate of decrease per cent., assuming it to have been uniform between the successive censuses.' Use such tabulated data to detect large declines (e.g. 68% decrease over forty years) and to time the onset of diminution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish decreased fertility from increased mortality
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether population decline is due chiefly to reduced birth rates (lessened fertility) or to elevated death rates (mortality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites direct evidence such as low average children per married couple (e.g. 'average of half a child to each married couple'), the proportion of married women who have ever borne children, and unusually high child mortality. He argues that such fertility measures can explain long-term decline even when episodic mortality events exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sex-ratio anomalies as diagnostic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine ratios of males to females (at birth and across ages) for abnormalities relative to civilized norms as possible indicators of reproductive dysfunction or social factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes an excess of male births in some island populations (e.g. 125.36 males per 100 females in the 1872 census) and uses this alongside fertility and mortality data to infer underlying demographic problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal correlation with cultural/habit changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether timing of population changes coincides with the introduction of new habits, foods, clothing, or other cultural changes (often via contact with Europeans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin points out that diminution began between 1830 and 1840 in several cases and links this to changes such as the introduction of new foods (maize steeped till putrid), European dress, tobacco, alcohol, and other altered practices. Temporal coincidence strengthens the hypothesis that changed habits affected fertility and health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh multiple causal hypotheses (disease, labour, morals) and compare plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: List and critically evaluate candidate causes—introduced diseases, wars, severe labour, supposed female profligacy—assessing which best fit the quantitative and qualitative evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin acknowledges that wars, labour, and diseases can cause rapid declines but argues that in many island cases these causes alone are insufficient; diminished fertility often better explains sustained decreases. Consider which causes explain both timing and patterns (e.g. child weakness, sex ratios).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical inference from animals' reproductive responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use evidence from domesticated and wild animals about susceptibility of the reproductive system to changed conditions as a model for human responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin marshals examples (tamed elephants not breeding in India, American monkeys rarely breeding in captivity, sterile cases after capture) to argue that slight changes in conditions often reduce fertility and produce weak or malformed offspring. Such analogies support the hypothesis that savages subjected to changed habits may become sterile or have weak young.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test correlations by empirical data collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose and use simple systematic data-gathering procedures to test hypothesized correlations (e.g., between hair/skin colour and susceptibility to tropical diseases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin proposed sending a blank table to army surgeons to count hair-colour categories in regiments and record disease incidence, to determine whether dark hair correlated with lower rates of malarious/yellow fevers. He emphasizes tabulation over anecdote and the need for many cases before drawing conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate effects of intercrossing (hybridization) on fertility and vigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether crossing with other races or populations increases or restores fertility and health in previously declining groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites the mixed Tahitian–English population that flourished (Pitcairn/Norfolk Islanders) and contrasts this with pure aboriginal declines, using such cases to argue that crossbreeding with 'civilised' races can confer immunity to harms of changed conditions and increase population growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject long-term inbreeding as the default explanation when timing contradicts it
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume that inbreeding/inter-breeding caused infertility if infertility closely follows contact with outsiders; compare to other communities with close kin marriage that remain fertile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues that infertility often coincides with European arrival, making prolonged inbreeding an unlikely explanation; he contrasts cases (Norfolk Islanders, Todas, Western Isles of Scotland) where close relationships do not show similar fertility loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geographic and historical distribution to test climatic/environmental causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare racial traits across diverse climates and consider duration of residence to judge whether direct environmental effects account for differences (e.g., skin colour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes that black and fair races occupy similar or diverse climates and that long-resident groups (e.g., Dutch families in South Africa) fail to change colour rapidly. Such distributional evidence weakens simple climate-based explanations for racial differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish direct effects of use/disuse and correlated development from selection explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether observed structural differences can be explained by altered use of parts, correlated developmental changes, or require selection (natural or sexual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin considers examples (stunted legs from canoe-life, enlarged chests at high altitudes, jaw size reduced by food habits) but judges these causes usually insufficient for major racial differences; correlated development (e.g., muscle and brow-ridge) may explain some features but not the whole pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider sexual selection as a plausible agent for differences between races
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether traits (colour, hairiness, form of features) are of the kind that could be modified by mate choice and thus fixed by sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin does not claim sexual selection explains everything but argues it has plausibility for many racial differences; he recommends reviewing the animal kingdom to estimate its likely effects and admits residual unexplained variation.
